title: Discourses close
hook: forty lessons from a blunt, kind teacher who was once a slave

segments.voice: Yesterday: prosochē, attention, the watchfulness you keep coming back to. Did you attend to one task from start to finish? Day four hundred thirty. The last day of the Discourses.

Most of us had one teacher who was hard on us and somehow, at the same time, obviously on our side. The one who handed back the paper covered in red ink and then stayed after class to go through it line by line. You may not have thanked them. Most people don't, until years later. For about forty days we've sat in a classroom in Nicopolis with a teacher like that. Today we stand up from the bench, look back at the room, and say goodbye. Today: the Discourses close.
screen: `THE RED-INK TEACHER.` → `FORTY DAYS IN NICOPOLIS.` → `THE DISCOURSES CLOSE.`

segments.voice: First, the man. Epictetus grew up enslaved, walked with a lame leg, and taught in a small school on the Greek coast after the emperor drove philosophers out of Rome. His name, Epiktetos, is usually said to mean acquired, a name for someone who was bought. He wrote nothing. What we have, his student Arrian took down: four books of talks, the Discourses, out of what was probably more. Second, the voice. He's blunt. He mocks, he teases, he calls his students lazy and their excuses silly. He'll ask a grieving father whether he left the room because he loved his child too much or too little. And he's kind in the way a good coach is kind: he refuses to let you be less than you could be. Third, what we carried out of the room. Look back: the gift of use, and not even Zeus can take your choice. Test the coin. Play the ball well. Who am I here. Habits grow by use. Found doing this. Alone, not lonely, the scout, in its season, at home here, nothing to take, my post, and yesterday, attention. One idea turned forty ways: some things are ours and some aren't, and freedom lives on the side that's ours. Fourth, the road ahead. Tomorrow a very different Stoic picks up the thread. Seneca was rich, powerful and close to an emperor, the opposite of a freed slave in a one-room school, and late in life he wrote letters to a friend. Same porch, new voice. But first, the thank you.
screen: `ENSLAVED, LAME, A TEACHER.` · `BLUNT AND KIND, LIKE A COACH.` · `FORTY WAYS INTO ONE IDEA.` · `NEXT: SENECA'S LETTERS.` · then, large: `THANK YOU, TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Take something to write on. Picture Epictetus on his bench in Nicopolis, an old man with a stick, students crowding the room. Now write him one line. Maybe what you'll keep. Maybe an argument you still want to have with him. Maybe just thank you. Keep it short and honest. Then read it back once, slowly, and let it stand. If a different teacher comes to mind, a real one from your own life, let them have a line too. The bell holds the time.
Discourses close. The end of about forty days with Epictetus, the freed slave and blunt, kind teacher whose talks Arrian wrote down. Today's word.
Your line: thank you, teacher. Keep your line to Epictetus somewhere you'll see it. And if a living teacher shaped you, today might be a good day to tell them. Day four hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Readers of Epictetus often reread the Discourses over many years, keeping a few lines close, and some write back to him in journals as if to a teacher.

fork.setup: a student tells Epictetus he left his sick child's room because he loved her too much to watch. what does Epictetus do?
options: asks whether that was really love, and presses him to think it through.
tells him to stop coming to class.
fork.reveal: in book one he questions the father until it's clear the leaving came from his own judgment, not from love: blunt, and meant to help.

original.note: Greek: the teacher's name, usually said to mean acquired or gained, a name given to an enslaved person.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Discourses are a book Epictetus wrote.
what it means: they're his talks, taken down by his student Arrian, from a blunt, kind teacher who had been enslaved.
what a scholar hears: four books survive; Photius in the ninth century mentions eight, so part of the Discourses is probably lost.
